# Version control with Git and GitHub {#sec-m5-git}

A reproducible report without a version history is half reproducibility. The code
regenerates the result, but nobody knows **which** code produced the number that went into the March
technical note, nor what changed between it and the June one.

Git solves this. It stores each state of the project as a *commit*: a snapshot with a
date, an author and a sentence saying what changed and why. GitHub is the place where these
snapshots are kept outside your machine, and where other people can access them.

::: {.callout-note}
## Git is not GitHub

**Git** is the program, installed on your computer, that records the history. It works without
internet. **GitHub** is a web service that hosts Git repositories. You can use Git without
GitHub; not the other way round.
:::

## Why this matters in the public sector

Three situations every technical officer has lived through:

1. **"Which version was sent?"** A folder with `analise_final.R`, `analise_final_v2.R`,
   `analise_final_v2_revisado_JOAO.R`. With Git, there is a single file, and the history says which
   state was delivered on each date.
2. **"The number changed and nobody knows why."** Git shows, line by line, what was
   changed between two versions, by whom and when.
3. **"The person who did it left the team."** The repository stays, with the code, the history
   and the messages explaining each decision.

It is the **trail** that spreadsheets and clicks in QGIS do not leave.

## Installation and setup

Install Git from <https://git-scm.com/downloads>. On an institutional machine, request it together with
R and RStudio (@sec-m1-ambiente). Then restart RStudio and check in RStudio's **terminal**
(the *Terminal* tab, not the *Console*):

```bash
git --version
```

Set your name and e-mail once. The `usethis` package does this from inside R:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))

usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "your.email@transportes.gov.br"
)
```
:::


To push to GitHub, RStudio needs a **personal access token**, which replaces the
password:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
usethis::create_github_token()   # opens GitHub in the browser to generate the token
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()         # paste the token when asked
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## The token is a password

Do not paste the *token* into a script, an AI *chat* or an e-mail. `gitcreds` stores it in the
system's credential manager, which is the right place.
:::

## Putting a project under version control

With the project open in RStudio:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
usethis::use_git()      # starts the local repository and offers the first commit
usethis::use_github()   # creates the repository on GitHub and pushes everything
```
:::


Restart RStudio when asked. A **Git** tab will appear in the top-right panel.

## The day-to-day cycle

All work with Git is this cycle, repeated:

| Step | In RStudio (Git tab) | In the terminal |
|:--|:--|:--|
| See what changed | the list of files with M (modified) or ? (new) | `git status` |
| Choose what goes in | tick the *Staged* box | `git add arquivo.R` |
| Record | **Commit** button, write the message | `git commit -m "message"` |
| Send to GitHub | **Push** button (green up arrow) | `git push` |
| Bring from GitHub | **Pull** button (blue down arrow) | `git pull` |

**A commit is local. Push is what sends it.** You can make several commits during the day and a
single push at the end. Nothing leaves your computer until the push.

### Commit messages that are good for something

The message is for whoever reads the history a year from now, possibly you.

| Bad | Good |
|:--|:--|
| `tweaks` | `Fix VISUM veh-km unit (it came in metres)` |
| `final version` | `Restrict delay to the structural network, exclude connectors` |
| `update` | `Update Comex Stat to 2025 and redo the municipality lookup` |

A good message says **what** changed and, when it is not obvious, **why**.

## What **not** to version

This is the most important part of the chapter for people working in the public sector.

Everything pushed to a **public** repository on GitHub is accessible to anyone,
and stays in the history even if it is deleted later. Deleting the file in a later commit does not
remove what has already been published.

Never version:

- **Non-public data.** Exports of contracted models, datasets with personal data,
  spreadsheets of ongoing studies. The VISUM export from @sec-m1-modelo4etapas is the
  course's example: it can only go into a public repository with express authorisation.
- **Credentials.** Passwords, *tokens*, connection *strings*. Use environment variables
  (`usethis::edit_r_environ()`).
- **Large raw data**, which are downloaded by a script. Version the script, not the file.
- **Generated files**, which the code recreates: results folders, Quarto's `_site/`,
  `renv/library/`.

The `.gitignore` file at the project root lists what Git should ignore. An excerpt of this
course's file:

```
# Quarto
/_site/
/.quarto/

# R
.Rproj.user/
.Rhistory
.RData

# data downloaded by script
/dados/brutos/
```


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
usethis::use_git_ignore("dados/brutos/")   # adds a line to .gitignore
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## A private repository for anything internal

GitHub allows **private** repositories, visible only to whoever you invite. For the Ministry's internal
analysis, that is the default, and it still gives you the history and the *backup*. Make public
only what is really meant for publication.
:::

## Looking at the history

The clock button in the Git tab opens the history. Clicking on a commit, you see exactly which
lines changed. In the terminal:

```bash
git log --oneline          # the list of commits, one line each
git diff                   # what changed since the last commit
git diff HEAD~1 analise.R  # what changed in a file since the second-to-last commit
```

## From repository to website

This material is a Git repository published as a website by GitHub Pages. The same goes for
any Quarto report (@sec-m5-quarto): each push to the main branch can
trigger the regeneration of the site, with no manual step. It is the natural conclusion of what the
course teaches: the code produces the result, Git records the history, and publishing is
automatic.

## Exercise

1. Put your final project under version control with `usethis::use_git()`.
2. Write a `.gitignore` that excludes the raw data and any non-public data.
3. Make three commits, each with a message explaining what changed and why.
4. Create a **private** repository on GitHub and push the project.
5. Open the history and find, in the *diff* of one of the commits, the line you changed.
